It must take at least twice as many hours as Cross-Track Capstone #3

prompt: Why does running a full nmap -p- scan per host sequentially become a real performance liability once the AD recon scanner is scaled from a 3-host lab to a realistic 30-50 host engagement?
choices: nmap cannot scan more than three hosts in a single invocation under any configuration
Per-host scan time stays roughly the same, but sequential execution makes total time grow linearly (or worse, with slow hosts) with host count, which can blow through a time-boxed engagement window
The packaging library used for version comparison cannot parse Windows service banners at all
nmap requires a graphical interface once more than one target is specified

prompt: In an Architecture Decision Record, what is the purpose of the 'Alternatives Considered' section?
choices: To list every tool the author has ever used, for completeness
To document other real options that were seriously evaluated and explicitly rejected, with the specific reasons why, so a future reader doesn't have to re-litigate the decision from scratch
To describe only the chosen option in more technical detail
To list features planned for some future version of the tool

prompt: What concurrency approach does ADR-004 choose for the multi-host AD recon scan, and why?
choices: Fully sequential scanning, because performance doesn't matter during reconnaissance
One unbounded thread per host, since real AD engagements never exceed a handful of hosts

A bounded worker pool (ThreadPoolExecutor with max_workers=8) wrapping per-host nmap invocations, trading some raw speed for not overwhelming the lab network or resembling a denial-of-service against the client's own systems
Rewriting nmap itself in pure Python to eliminate subprocess calls entirely

choices: Confirming that vulncheck.py prints the right CVE for one known test banner
An ADR explaining why bounded concurrent scanning was chosen over a single combined nmap invocation and over unbounded concurrency, with the rejected alternatives and their consequences recorded
